displayQuote: One death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic

meta.title: Who really said "One death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stalin. No Soviet source of any kind exists. The saying appears in a French satirical paper in March 1924, attributed there to an unnamed Quai d'Orsay diplomat, and in German in Kurt Tucholsky's 1925 essay. The Stalin credit begins with a 1947 Leonard Lyons column.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'One death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic'?
meta.ogDescription: No Stalin source exists. The line is French, printed in March 1924, and was pinned on Stalin by an American gossip columnist in January 1947.

answer.label: Not Stalin — an anonymous French remark of 1924
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest located printing 6 March 1924, in French
answer.sourceLine: There is no Stalin source. It is not in his collected works, his speeches or the Soviet record, and Russian historians have not found it. The earliest located printing is the French satirical paper Comic-Finance of 6 March 1924, where it is put in the mouth of an unnamed diplomat of the Quai d’Orsay inside what appears to be an invented anecdote. Kurt Tucholsky gave a German version in 1925 — explicitly as a French joke he was passing on, not as his own line. The Stalin attribution first appears in the United States in 1947.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None — no document, speech or record

source.excerpt: The death of one man is, indeed, a terrible thing, but one hundred thousand deaths is a statistic.
trail: The 1924 French printing is the earliest instance anyone has located. It is not a report of something a named person said — it is an anecdote, probably fictional, in which a Foreign Ministry diplomat delivers the line. Two further French writers repeated it in April 1924 without naming an author, which is what you would expect of a joke already in circulation.

Kurt Tucholsky put a German form of it into print in 1925: ‘Der Tod eines Menschen: das ist eine Katastrophe. Hunderttausend Tote: das ist eine Statistik!’ Because it was later anthologised, Tucholsky is himself sometimes given as the author — wrongly. He was quoting, and the essay’s title says so German quotation research ↗.

The Stalin attribution is traceable to a single American newspaper column: Leonard Lyons, in the Washington Post, 30 January 1947. Lyons offered no source and no occasion beyond a bare claim that Stalin had said it. Everything since — the quotation dictionaries, the memes, the epigraphs — descends from that column the documented chain ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located wording, translated from the French of March 1924. Note the numbers: one hundred thousand, not a million. The inflation to a million happens later, in English, and is part of how the saying acquired a Soviet accent.

sourceLink.text: The documented chain from 1924 to the 1947 Stalin credit

source.rightsNote: The 1924 French printing is anonymous and long out of copyright, and Kurt Tucholsky died in 1935, so his 1925 German text has been public domain in the EU since 2006. The saying as given here is free to reproduce. One caution: Leonard Lyons’s 1947 column is a separate work whose US status depends on renewal and which we have not resolved — quote the 1924 line, not the column. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Joseph Stalin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Stalin
author.metaLine: 1878–1953 · General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party, 1922–1952
author.bio: Joseph Stalin presided over a state whose deaths are genuinely counted in the millions — the famine of 1932–33, the Great Terror, the camps — which is precisely why a cold aphorism about mass death sticks to him so easily. The attribution works as a kind of shorthand: the line sounds like an admission, and the admission sounds like him. But sounding like someone is not evidence, and the language of the Soviet record is not where this sentence comes from. It arrived in English through a 1947 gossip column, and the column cited nothing.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Four separate names circulate as the author. One is a newspaper joke of 1924, and the rest are later readers mistaking a quotation for a coinage.

items.why: Nothing in the collected works, the speeches, the stenographic records or the archives. The credit begins with a Washington Post column of 30 January 1947 by Leonard Lyons, who cited nothing and dated the supposed remark to 1933.

items.who: Real text, but he was quoting
items.why: Tucholsky printed a German version in 1925 under the heading ‘Französischer Witz’ — French wit. He was passing on a French joke, and the French printing predates him by a year. Anthologies later stripped the framing, and he is now sometimes credited with it outright.

Mary Soames, Churchill’s daughter, recalled hearing Stalin say something like it at Potsdam in July 1945. That is a recollection of a conversation, published long afterwards, and it postdates the printed French version by twenty-one years. Even if accurate, it would make Stalin a repeater, not an author.
The 1924 French has ‘one hundred thousand.’ English versions say a million, or millions. There is no fixed text, which is itself a sign of an oral saying rather than a quotation from a document.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous French remark, printed 6 March 1924 and repeated in German by Tucholsky in 1925. The Stalin credit dates from a single unsourced American newspaper column of 30 January 1947 the chain ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The observation itself is sound, and has since been measured: people give more, and feel more, for one identified victim than for a large number of unidentified ones. Psychologists call it the identifiable victim effect. That is why the line survives detachment from any author — it describes something real about how attention works.

The attribution is doing separate work. Put in Stalin’s mouth, a description of a human limitation becomes a confession of policy: not this is how we fail to feel but this is how I counted. That reversal is the whole appeal of the misattribution, and it is the reason the line is quoted far more often than it is checked.
detailsBody: 6 March 1924 — Comic-Finance, Paris, prints the line as the remark of an unnamed Quai d’Orsay diplomat, inside an apparently invented anecdote.
April 1924 — two further French writers repeat it without naming an author.
1925 — Kurt Tucholsky prints a German version, framed explicitly as French wit.
30 January 1947 — Leonard Lyons, Washington Post, attributes it to Stalin without evidence and dates it to 1933.
After 1947 — the Stalin credit enters quotation dictionaries and never leaves.
context.pull: The 1924 French says one hundred thousand. The million arrives later, in English, with Stalin's name attached.
